==English==

===Pronunciation===
* {{q|stressed}}
** {{IPA|en|/ˌəʊˈkeɪ/|a=RP}}

===Etymology 1===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*h₂el- (other)||*h₃reǵ-}}
Origin {{unk|en|title=disputed}}. Wikipedia lists {{w|List of proposed etymologies of OK|many possible etymologies}}, of which the most widely accepted is that it is an abbreviation of {{m|en|oll korrect|oll/orl korrect}}, a comical spelling of {{m|en|all correct}}, which first appeared in print in ''The Boston Morning Post'' on March 23, 1839, as part of a fad for similar fanciful abbreviations in the United States during the late 1830s. The expression became popular through its use in the presidential campaign of Martin Van Buren in 1840, who was nicknamed {{m|en|Old Kinderhook}}, and then slowly acquired other meanings.<ref name="npr">{{cite-web |en |url=https://www.npr.org/2025/07/23/nx-s1-5463788/ok-origin-martin-van-buren |title=OK, is Martin Van Buren responsible for the tiny word that punches above its weight? |work={{w|All Things Considered}} |first=Scott |last=Neuman |date=2025-07-23 |accessdate=2025-07-23|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20260926075952/https://www.npr.org/2025/07/23/nx-s1-5463788/ok-origin-martin-van-buren|archivedate=26 September 2026}}</ref>

The {{cog|cho|-}} word {{m|cho|oke}}, {{m|cho|okeh||it is so}}, common in Choctaw translations of the Bible, could also explain ''OK''{{'}}s variety of affirmative definitions. Additionally, ''{{lang|cho|okeh}}'' was the most common etymology of ''okay'' in dictionaries until the 1960s, and linguistically predates Boston's ''O.K.''. However, this theory suffers from the fact that the Choctaw language was relatively obscure and generally spoken (sometimes in a [[pidgin]] form) mainly with African-American slaves.

# {{non-gloss|Used to introduce a sentence in order to draw attention to the importance of what is being said.}}

#: {{ux|en|'''OK''', I'm thinking of a number…}}
# {{non-gloss|Used in {{w|turn-taking}}, serving as a request to the speaker to grant the turn to the interrupter.}}
#: {{ux|en|You always do this to me! When we were at your mother’s, you said that…  – '''OK''', '''OK''', …}}
# {{non-gloss|Used to sarcastically or sardonically indicate agreement with the previous statement.}}
